description: We are interested in health and data science.
summary:
On long space missions, an astronaut's spine changes. In microgravity it stretches, the back muscles weaken and back pain is common. When the crew returns to gravity, those changes raise the risk of injury, and the astronaut has to notice the warning signs without a doctor nearby, often with a slow or unreliable link to Earth.

Today there is no simple way for a crew member to watch their own spine health day by day, so small changes go unseen until they become a problem.

Asclepius Orbit is a light wearable harness and a tablet app that do this for them. The harness measures how much the spine lengthens, how it moves and how hard the back muscles work. The app turns those measurements into one clear signal, green, amber or red, explains the reasons in plain language, suggests the next step and prepares a report for the flight surgeon on the ground. It works completely offline, so it keeps helping even when contact with Earth is lost.

Our goal is to help astronauts catch spine problems early, stay protected during the mission and prepare a safe return to Earth's gravity.
details:
Overview

We have 2 main branches of our project: Software and Hardware, described below.

Hardware

The hardware part consists of 3 sensors each measuring a different parameter that can lead to good relations and reasonable results.

Stretch cord: spine elongation

The conductive resistive rubber consists of an elastic band that will be sticked to the user's backbone going from C3 (cervical vertebrate 3) to L5 (lumbar vertebrate 5), when this rubber gets longer the resistance between the terminals of the rope increases, with this we can relate the electrical resistance increase with the elongation.

IMU: range of motion

Second of all, we have the IMU, it is basically a tracker of movement and rotation, so we can appreciate the range of movement of the astronaut while exercising or while being at rest, being able to compare the physical metrics of the backbone on Earth vs Space, for instance, if the astronaut's stay is long enough we might be able to see that the lumbar curve starts to soften.

EMG: muscle effort and fatigue

At last we have the EMG, with 3 electrodes connected 2 connected to each dorsal muscle and the third to a GND, this sensor can detect the muscle activity, helping to know the effort required for a certain physical task and being able to notice the muscle wear throughout the exercise.

Why this architecture

A spine monitor for a spacecraft has to be trustworthy, not just clever. Every layer of the system below answers a real constraint of long space missions.

  • Offline by design: everything, including the language model, runs on board, so nothing depends on a ground link or a cloud service and no health data leaves the vehicle.
  • Safe by construction: the AI assistant reads the data only through read-only tools, must call a tool before stating any fact, never diagnoses, and a deterministic fallback keeps answering if the model fails. Red-flag symptoms escalate immediately, whatever the model says.
  • Explainable: every green, amber or red verdict comes with the signals that drove it, its confidence and the data that is missing, instead of a black-box score.
  • Personal: each astronaut is compared with their own preflight baseline, because normal spine length and muscle activity differ from person to person.
  • Robust to real sensors: signal-quality flags, packet loss, reboots and clock drift are handled and tested with a simulator that injects those faults on purpose, so the system degrades gracefully instead of raising false alarms.
  • Verifiable: contract-first interfaces, a 90% coverage gate, mutation testing, property-based tests and API fuzzing, because a health tool has to be tested far beyond the happy path.

Software

All the software is open source in our public repository (https://github.com/Asclepius-Orbit/nasa-hackathon) and runs fully on board, with no cloud service. It is built contract-first: JSON Schema, OpenAPI and AsyncAPI contracts generate the Python and TypeScript types, so every component exchanges the same validated messages.

  1. Firmware (Arduino Uno/Nano, C++). It samples the EMG at 1000 Hz, the IMU (MPU-6050) at 100 Hz and the stretch cord at 20 Hz with timer interrupts, and sends CRC-protected ASCII frames over USB serial at 9600 baud.
  2. Python gateway. It reads the serial frames, checks the CRC, assembles them into signal chunks, handles calibration and commands, and publishes everything to MQTT with QoS 1, a last will and reconnection with backoff.
  3. MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto). An authenticated broker with per-device ACLs. Topics follow asclepius/v1/crew/{astronaut}/device/{device}/{stream, status, clock, calibration, ack, cmd}, and every payload is validated against a JSON Schema.
  4. Simulator. A mission generator that simulates the three sensors together with microgravity, exercise, fatigue, deconditioning and realistic faults (lead-off, motion artifacts, packet loss, reboots), and writes the ground truth. It replaces the hardware in the same pipeline, so the whole system can be demonstrated and tested without the wearable.
  5. Backend (FastAPI, SQLite). It ingests and validates the telemetry, removes duplicate chunks, sends commands to the device, stores sessions, self-reports and assessments, produces a PDF report for ground control, and serves the app, with Server-Sent Events for live repetition counting. A separate read-only API serves the AI assistant.
  6. Hybrid predictive engine (FastAPI, stateless). It extracts features from the signals (EMG amplitude, left-right symmetry and spectral fatigue, IMU range of motion, cord elongation and recovery, symptoms), builds a personal baseline for each astronaut and protocol, and scores deviations with robust z-scores. CUSUM and Kalman detectors must agree before a change counts as sustained. The changes feed a saturating risk score, and a declarative triage policy with red-flag symptoms gives a green, amber or red status with the reasons, the confidence and recommendations. A what-if endpoint projects a feature forward with a linear fit. It is decision support, not a validated clinical model, and its thresholds are provisional.
  7. MCP server (Model Context Protocol, stdio). Eight read-only tools: search_evidence, get_current_status, get_history, get_sessions, get_self_reports, compare_periods, explain_assessment and simulate_scenario.
  8. Local AI assistant. An agent (pydantic-ai) runs on the astronaut's own machine with Ollama and the Qwen3.5 4B model, so no data leaves the vehicle and no connection is needed. It must call a tool before stating any fact, never computes numbers itself, never diagnoses, refers clinical questions to the flight surgeon, and falls back to a deterministic summary if the model fails. A code guard flags diagnostic claims, and a regression suite of 32 evaluation cases in English, Spanish and Catalan checks this behaviour (the chosen model passed 26 of 32).
  9. Desktop app (Electron, React, TypeScript). The on-board tablet app: a PIN login for each crew member; a Today screen with the spine figure and the green, amber or red verdict with its reasons; a one-minute daily report; guided exercise sessions with live repetition counting; a 30-day history with charts; an Ask Asclepius chat with the assistant; an urgent-symptom button; a preflight baseline; and a report for ground control. The app is hardened with a sandbox, a strict content security policy, validated IPC and no network access in the renderer.

Quality and testing

Test-driven development, a 90% line and branch coverage gate, mutation testing, property-based tests, API fuzzing from the OpenAPI contracts, golden snapshots and continuous integration on every pull request.

Project status

The full pipeline runs end to end with the simulator and an Arduino emulator. The firmware builds and its serial protocol is tested against golden lines, but the real sensor signals have not yet been verified end to end on the hardware. The simulated signals use placeholder physiological values, and the clinical thresholds are expert proposals that still need clinical validation.

Use of Super Intelligence (AI)

Code, tests and documentation were written with AI coding assistants: Claude Code (Claude Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and Fable models), Codex (Luna, Terra and Sol models) and Gemini (4 Hydrogen). The team designed the system, reviewed the work and ran it. At runtime, the on-board assistant uses the Qwen3.5 4B language model through Ollama. The Asclepius Orbit logo was generated with AI (OpenAI); wherever it appears on this page it carries a visible "AI-generated" mark. No other image, video or audio was generated with AI, and no NASA logos or branding are used.
